#8042. Is That Really A Service Dog?

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person.  The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

This is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

Sir Terry Pratchett famously declared that cats remember when they were worshipped as gods, and it makes sense; our feline friends have an extra-special hold on our hearts – so much so that, yeah, we 100% want to know our birth month cat.

If you're one of those people who spends a lot of time reading up on how to make your yard more appealing to your cats (or which plants that are poisonous for cats) rather than tips on how to repel the neighborhood's kitties, then chances are you've wondered which cat breed best matches your personality at least once. At least.

It makes a lot of sense, too; after all, from playful kitties to lap cats that just want to be left alone to their sunbeam, there is an incredible amount of variety to be found in the feline kingdom. And after looking at our birth month pets, I couldn't resist taking a closer look at cats in particular...

I know, I know; we’re already familiar with the idea of a birth month bird, birth month animal, birth month owl, and birth month bug, but cats are particularly brilliant if you want to match a critter up with your personality.

Whether you're a determined January baby, a dreamy June soul or a fiercely independent November personality, there's a feline to match your character. And so, from adventurous Bengals to affectionate ragdolls, here are all 12 birth months matched to the cat breeds that best capture their personality traits.

Grab yourself a packet of catmint seeds, then, and get ready to find out which cat matches your birth month...

If you're a January baby, you're known for being ambitious, independent and determined. It should come as no surprise, then, that the Maine Coon is your birth month cat; after all, these striking kitties have a confident presence, are intelligent and have a reputation for being independent-minded.

A natural leader of the cat world? Sound about right!

February belongs to the Abyssinian, which makes a lot of sense when you think about it. Just like the creative, curious and intelligent people born at this time of year, Abyssinians are famously inquisitive, playful and adventurous.

In other words, these kitties are true free spirits. Sound familiar?

March babies are quiet, sensitive and introspective – but don't let the fact that they're not the loudest in the room fool you. Especially as their birth month cat is an elegant beauty who's often reserved around strangers but affectionate with their trusted people.

Basically, the Russian Blue is a perfect match for March's gentle and imaginative personality for a reason. And, if this has struck a nerve with you, then why not honor your birth month cat further with this Russian Blue Calendar 2027?

Bold, adventurous and full of charisma, April belongs to one of the more unusual members of the cat family: the Bengal. Unlike many cats that absolutely abhor water, these pretty kitties absolutely love it – almost as much as they love exploring. This, coupled with their energetic and confident natures, means they're not exactly known for sitting quietly on the sidelines! (Sound familiar?)

One of the most iconic cat breeds going, May's birth month cat is the sociable, expressive and strong-willed Siamese.

With their bright blue eyes and unusual coloring, these kitties are among the most instantly recognizable breeds in the US. They're also famously vocal and people-oriented, with plenty of personality to keep everyone entertained... just like May babies.

If you're a June baby, you're romantic, sensitive and affectionate. No surprises, then, that your birth month cat is the beautiful ragdoll! These gorgeous kitties are known for their gentle souls, their people-loving natures and their tendency to follow their favorite humans around the house.

Essentially, they're a lovely fit for June's dreamy and sentimental side. And they go all floppy like a ragdoll when you pick them up, making them excellent snugglers, too!

If you're a July baby, you're curious, private and quietly determined – and you tend to prefer a small but loyal friendship group to a big and sprawling one. Enter, then, one of the cutest birth month cats on this list: the Birman!

Loyal, loving and family-oriented. Birmans are often affectionate and sociable without being excessively demanding. They're the comforting presence of the feline family, basically, so lean into it!

Born in the height of summer, August babies tend to be every bit as sunny-natured as you think they'd be – think confident, outgoing and full of character. They certainly know how to command attention, and all hail that kind of chaotic energy, quite frankly!

September's long been associated with successful leaders, which means those born under this month tend to be practical, composed and deeply intelligent. Their birth month cats are similar, as British Shorthairs are generally calm, independent and undemanding.

They appreciate a routine and like things just so, but they like it that way for a reason – and it's why they're one of the most popular cats around, as it makes for a cuddly and serene companion.

October babies, assemble! While some might expect those born in the spookiest month of all to be assigned a birth month cat like the hairless Sphynx cat, think again!

Turkish Angoras are intelligent, playful and often quite determined. They have a flair for the dramatic, too, making them an ideal match for passionate, expressive and sociable October-born folk everywhere. (Although, admittedly, this 'I Like A Handful Of Humans And My Turkish Angora' Mug is giving pure Scorpio energy!).

Wannabe witches, rejoice! November babies get the beautiful Bombay cat, which might be the most mysterious member of this list of birth month cats. Why? Well, because with their glossy black coats and striking eyes, these kitties have an enigmatic appearance, while often being deeply affectionate with their chosen people.

If this is your birth month cat, you're mysterious, intuitive and quietly determined... and a brilliant person to have in anyone's corner, quite frankly.

Last but not least, December babies are known for being adventurous, energetic and fun-loving – and generous of spirit enough to be able to deal with the fact that their birthday falls smack-bang in the middle of the holidays.

Somalis, then, make their ideal birth month cat, as they are curious, playful and love exploring their surroundings. (As an added bonus, they're simply stunning, too!).

Ernest Hemingway famously declared that “a cat has absolute emotional honesty: human beings, for one reason or another, may hide their feelings, but a cat does not.” Whichever birth month cat you call your own, then, try to follow its good example and be more in touch with your true feelings and self.

Remember, too, that you don't have to own a cat (does anybody truly own a cat, after all?) to enjoy seeing them in your garden; plant up some cat-friendly plants, and watch the kitties go to town. Just be sure to keep bird feeders up and out of their way, yeah?

My 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

My dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an issue for me right now.â

Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is important to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Talk to your vet about a payment plan, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most important first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

Although hydrangea flowerheads can look pretty framed against a winter landscape, it’s important not to leave them to their own devices this month. Make a little time in November for these care essentials

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As November arrives, backyard activity may be slowing, but beneath the surface, hydrangeas are entering a critical transition. As day length shortens and the air gets fresher and nippier, deciduous shrubs shift their energy into the roots. Understanding exactly what to do (and not do) for hydrangeas now begins with recognizing that dormant plants are still susceptible to moisture stress and sub-zero cold.

Obviously, not all hydrangeas are the same. Some form buds on old wood, which means pruning now is a no-no. Other types are hardier than others, and so need less winter protection. So in order to give hydrangeas the best winter care, you must first know exactly which type of hydrangea you have. However, these November care tips can all help to make a big difference to next year’s display.

Taking action this month gives you enormous benefits in the approach to the colder months ahead. Taking time now can help you shield key dormant buds from bitter cold, adjust water levels, stabilize and protect roots, and ensure your plants emerge stronger than ever next spring. So don’t chance it and leave your favorite shrubs unattended this month. Here are the crucial tasks to do before winter…

Effective fall care lies primarily in knowing your hydrangea type and variety. Varieties that bloom on old wood, such as bigleaf hydrangea (H. macrophylla) and oakleaf hydrangea (H. quercifolia) have already formed embryonic flower buds. If these buds freeze or are pruned off, next year's blooms will be tragically lost before you see them. Conversely, panicles (H. paniculata) and smooth hydrangeas (H. arborescens) produce flowers on new wood grown in spring, making them more resilient to frosts.

Popular bigleaf cultivars such as Nikko Blue or the Cityline series and serrated mountain hydrangeas need bud protection in cold zones. Cold-hardy panicle varieties like Limelight or Bobo and native smooth hydrangeas like Annabelle rarely require insulation, though they still benefit from consistent root hydration.

November hydrangea care also depends on your location, climate and USDA hardiness zone. Gardeners in northern zones 3-5 experience frozen ground and drying winter winds, demanding comprehensive stem barriers and thick thermal mulches. In contrast, those in southern zones 7-9 must contend with erratic temperature swings, where unseasonal late-fall warm spells can trick dormant buds into opening prematurely, only to be sheared by subsequent frosts.

Soil type also matters. Heavy clay soils hold water and risk winter ice pockets around roots, while light, sandy soils drain rapidly and dry out under frozen winds. Before tackling these tasks, it’s worth investing in a soil diagnostic tool with a long probe. The XLUX Deep Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon, gives instant readings to make better decisions before the first hard freeze. Don’t forget your trusty bypass pruners to remove any dead or damaged branches safely, plus some isopropyl alcohol to clean blades before and after use. You’re then ready to start…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

One of the kindest things you can do for your hydrangeas this month is to “think twice, cut once” when it comes to pruning. One of the biggest hydrangea mistakes is indiscriminately shearing back during fall cleanups. For old-wood bloomers like bigleaf, mountain, and oakleaf varieties, the buds that produce next summer’s flowers are already set near the tips of the stems. Pruning these in November removes those flower buds, reducing or eliminating next summer's blooms.

For these hydrangeas, you need to resist all structural shaping, topping, or cutting back until immediately after flowering finishes next year. The only exception is removing dead, diseased, or broken stems, which can be cut down to the base at any time. Use sharp bypass pruners like the Felco 2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon, for exceptional clean cuts.

Equally important is leaving the faded, papery flower heads all winter long. While it might be tempting to tidy up dried flower clusters on varieties like Endless Summer or PeeGee, these old blooms act as shields for the tender buds tucked beneath them. So it’s a good idea to leave them in place now. Dried flower clusters also add visual interest to the winter garden, especially when they collect small mounds of snow. Then, in late winter or early spring, as fresh green growth emerges at the base, you can snip the old flower heads off above the first set of green buds.

Hydrangeas need plenty of water, even now. While deciduous foliage yellows and drops, hydrangea roots take up moisture until the soil drops below freezing. Winter air and winds can be drying, and with the ground frozen, the roots cannot replace what gets lost. So don’t be tempted to put your hoses and watering cans away too early. Entering winter in dehydrated soil can lead to brittle branches and dead tips by spring. Get your hydrangeas as hydrated as possible before winter really begins.

If you’re having a rainy fall, you might not need to water hydrangeas, but check the soil and give your hydrangeas a good soaking as needed. If rainfall is sparse, provide a deep, slow soaking every 10-14 days. Aim to moisten the soil 8-12 inches (10-15cm) deep, encouraging roots to settle deeper underground. Prioritize any newly planted shrubs, which need more water as they get established.

Soaker hoses are great options for targeted and controlled watering. You can buy Expert Gardener 50ft Soaker Hoses from Walmart to help you direct the flow wherever you grow your hydrangeas. Stop supplemental watering once morning frosts result in frozen soil.

Soil temperatures fluctuate erratically during late fall and early winter. Rapid freeze-and-thaw cycles cause frost heave, where expanding and contracting soil pushes shallow root crowns above the soil line, exposing roots to drying winds and freezing cold air. You can give key hydrangeas a helping hand by giving them extra insulation this month. This stabilizes soil temperatures, preserves deep moisture, and protects delicate roots through winter.

Start by adding a top-dressing of compost This will slowly break down over winter, releasing micronutrients that enhance soil and slowly feed the roots. A great composting option at this time of year is mushroom compost. You can get lush ready-made bags of Espoma Natural Mushroom Blend Fertilizer, from Walmart, to prime the earth and provide steady support through the colder months.

The compost can do double duty as an insulating mulch, but you can also use other types of mulch, like shredded bark or chopped leaves. Add a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of coarse, loose mulch. I like Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help lock in late-season soil moisture and regulate soil temperature. Always leave a 2-inch (5cm) gap around the woody stems to reduce the risks of fungal rot and gnawing rodents.

If you’re in zones 4-6 growing bigleaf or oakleaf hydrangeas, sub-zero cold and winter winds pose a big threat to next year's blooms. As noted, old wood hydrangeas have flower buds now. While the roots may be hardy to zone 5, flower buds can suffer frostbite below 0°F (-18°C). If stems die back, old-wood varieties will produce foliage during the summer, but zero flowers. So depending on your hardiness zones, consider adding some physical protection if your winters are very cold.

Do this in late November, after the plant drops its leaves and enters dormancy. Drive four sturdy hardwood or metal stakes into the ground around your hydrangea. Keep them several inches clear of the branches. Then wrap breathable fabric around the outside of the stakes to make a wind barrier. Use burlap or jute, such as Wellco Gardening Burlap Roll from The Home Depot, to protect against biting winds while maintaining healthy air flow around the plant. Secure with zip ties or twine.

For extreme northern climates, you can construct a cylinder of wire fencing around the plant and loosely fill with dry pine needles or oak leaves. Just avoid packing the leaves tightly and never use plastic tarps, which trap condensation and bake tender stems on sunnier winter afternoons.

Hydrangeas in outdoor pots, ceramic planters, and decorative troughs require proactive winter care. Unlike in-ground plants, potted roots are exposed to freezing air on all sides. An unprotected container's soil temperature can be 20°F lower than the garden soil, putting roots at risk of freezing and killing the plant outright. Ceramic and terracotta pots also absorb water, making them susceptible to cracking when wet soil freezes and expands. So you’ll need to give your container-based hydrangeas more protection if you have very cold winters.

Begin by grouping potted hydrangeas together along a sheltered, south or east-facing foundation wall, out of wind corridors. Elevate your pots off cold concrete using pot feet or bricks to ensure drainage holes remain clear. Wrap the body of each pot in bubble wrap, thermal burlap, or foam insulation, securing the wrap beneath the outer rim without covering the top soil. You can also pick up floating plant jackets or anti-frost fleece covers, such as the Valibe Shrub Protection Plant Jacket from Amazon, which you can slip over potted hydrangeas in cold snaps.

If you are in zone 6 or colder, move your potted hydrangeas into an unheated garage, garden shed, or cold frame for the winter. These sheltered spaces keep plants dormant while protecting them from sub-zero drafts. Check on them once a month, providing a splash of water so the roots never completely dry out.

As well as the things you should be doing this month, preparing your hydrangeas for the colder months requires knowing what to avoid. We’ve touched on pruning certain hydrangea types. Avoid aggressive pruning on old-wood varieties like bigleaf and oakleaf hydrangeas, which shears away next summer's flower buds. Another thing to avoid doing is allowing roots to dry out prior to ground freeze, as desiccated roots are vulnerable. Keep watering if the soil is dry and remains unfrozen.

Never apply high-nitrogen fertilizers at this time of year. Feeding now forces a flush of soft, tender growth that cannot harden off before freezing weather strikes, causing stem dieback. Don’t use clear plastic sheeting or non-breathable tarps as winter wraps, as they trap humidity, promote mold, and create greenhouse heat spikes on sunny days. This can trick dormant buds into waking prematurely. Finally, don’t just assume all hydrangeas need the same winter protection. Know your hydrangea type, how far north it is hardy, and how far you need to intervene to keep yours healthy.

Taking a little time in November to protect your hydrangeas makes all the difference for the year ahead. By maintaining hydration, shielding exposed old-wood buds from freezing gales, and insulating roots with a mulch blanket, you give your prized shrubs the exact winter protection they need. Come spring, your hydrangeas will emerge from dormancy strong, healthy, and ready to produce a summer display of blooms.

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#8037. We Tested Home Generators to Find the Best Picks for a Power Outage

By Glenda Taylor, Austin Fracchia, Mark Wolfe, Zach Lazzari

Updated Nov 3, 2026 9:44 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

During a power outage, a home generator can keep the lights on, the HVAC running, and the appliances powered, but there are a lot of options out there, from whole-house to quiet inverter models. Because we’re big on helping our readers navigate the array of products that make life easier, our team tackled the task of testing home generators.

These independent power sources range in output for a variety of needs. After researching more than 40 top models, we selected the highest-scoring models in a range of categories for hands-on testing. Our favorite was the Champion 7500-Watt Dual-Fuel Generator thanks to its versatile operation and multiple outlets.

Whether you’re looking for a generator to run an entire home or to power only a few essentials, you can find a top-notch one in this lineup. Keep reading to find out how each one performed and to learn more about what to consider when shopping for the best home generator for your needs.

Bottom line: Our comprehensive testing reveals top home generators for every need, from budget-friendly to whole-house solutions.

When shopping for a generator, it’s easy to become overwhelmed by the available options on the market. While the following models vary in fuel type, electrical load, and intended use, each one earned a spot on this lineup by excelling in real-world tests.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 5/5

This Champion 7,500-watt dual-fuel generator delivers enough electricity to power up an off-grid jobsite or keep critical home circuits running through a utility outage. It includes numerous convenience features, like a push-button electric starter, covered outlets, and a fold-out transport handle. In our tests, the push-button starter worked perfectly, no matter the weather.

We appreciated its two locking 30A outlets (one 120V and one 120/240V) for powering a home, workshop, RV, or heavy-duty tools like portable welders. It also has four household-style 120V-20A outlets for lower-wattage applications. On a 7.7-gallon tank of gas, this generator supports a 50 percent load for up to 10 hours or up to 5.5 hours with a 20-pound propane cylinder. Using propane, we ran a portable table saw, miter saw, router, and air compressor for 4 hours and had just under half a tank of propane left over.

On the downside, its heavy weight made it tough to navigate across a yard and lift in and out of a truck. It also does not include an idle controller, which leads to more fuel consumption than eco-throttle-equipped generators. Still, it offered plenty of power and access points for the price.

Get the Champion 7500-watt home generator at Blain’s Farm & Fleet.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Power 4.5/5; Portability 5/5; Noise 4/5; Value 4.5/5

A no-frills dual-fuel generator that’s small enough to tuck away in the corner of a garage or in a truck bed, the Pulsar 2200-watt generator delivered an easy experience powering our test equipment. The 1.18-gallon generator can run for up to 8 hours on half load on a single tank of gas.

Setting up the generator for the first time was fairly straightforward, though filling the oil for the first time proved to be a challenge. The side panel that we needed to unscrew and pop off to access the oil fill port and dipstick was difficult to remove. We also had to lay the generator on its side to fill it with oil, which required a bit of balancing as it’s not completely flat. Balancing while pouring oil was a bit tricky, to say the least. Starting it was a piece of cake. Turning on the Pulsar requires pulling a recoil start, but the engine kicked on after just a couple of pulls—even in the cold.

We used several appliances, including a couple of heat guns and hair dryers at the same time to test the generator at different loads. As promised, the generator handled a combined 1,800 watts without much issue and shut power off when we overloaded it with 2,300 watts.

The Pulsar’s noise level seemed louder than expected, but it was still in a reasonable range for its output. It’s a great option for budget-priced backup power for light-duty power needs such as small DIY projects and powering a couple of household appliances during an outage.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 4.5/5; Value 4.5/5

It’s hard to beat Westinghouse’s 4,500-watt inverter generator for power output, versatility, and portability. It’s not the highest-wattage model we tested, but it excelled at running several power tools, including grinders and saws, as well as the essentials in our travel trailer. Setting it up was a snap—all we had to do was add oil and fill the gas tank. Best of all, it’s quiet and efficient.

While this would be a great emergency generator, we also think it’s a top-notch pick for RVs, camping, and remote powering due to its quiet and efficient operation.

The iGen4500 has a 3.4-gallon gasoline tank that can run up to 18 hours. Since it’s an inverter, it only burns enough to cover the appliances or tools it’s powering. This makes it more eco-friendly than noninverter models that burn fuel at a set rate no matter how much power is being drawn. This backup generator offers a variety of power ports, including a 30A port, two 20A ports, and two USB ports. However, it weighs almost 105 pounds without fuel, so lifting it up and down can be challenging for one person.

Read our full review: Westinghouse iGen4500 Inverter Generator

Get the Westinghouse home generator at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 4/5

The Honda EU2200i inverter generator offers reliability, simple operation, and low noise. Honda estimates that the EU2200i runs at 48 to 57 weighted decibels, and we found that its sound easily gets lost in the background. It comes equipped with a Honda GXR120 commercial series engine that delivers 120 volts and up to 1,800 running watts and 2,200 starting watts. A 125V-20A duplex outlet allows users to plug in two electrical cords without worrying about overloading the generator. T

his machine is compatible with the Honda My Generator mobile app for remote monitoring and is parallel-ready for use with a second Honda EU2200i (connection kit sold separately). It also features a built-in carbon monoxide sensor and safety shutoff. In two separate tests, we used the Honda generator to power a full-size refrigerator for 4 hours and then a portable table saw and miter saw for an 8-hour workday. We even added a USB hub to charge a phone and laptop.

In each test, the devices worked perfectly, the electrical current remained strong and steady, and the breaker didn’t trip. The generator’s molded plastic handle is well placed, and when combined with the machine’s proportions, the unit is fairly easy to carry, even though it weighs nearly 50 pounds. We would have appreciated a built-in USB port in addition to the wall-style outlet, though. As it was, we had to unplug a tool that draws 10A just to charge a device using less than 3A.

Still, a clean electrical current and quiet operation in a lightweight, easy-to-stow package make the Honda an excellent choice for a home backup generator.

Get the Honda home generator at Amazon or Northern Tool + Equipment.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Power 5/5; Portability 4/5; Noise 4/5; Value 4.5/5

Westinghouse WGen9500DF is an all-around top pick when the power goes out. It has a 6.6-gallon gasoline tank that will keep it running for 12 hours at 25 percent load and up to 8 hours at 50 percent load. (Actual tank runtime may vary depending on gasoline quality and electrical load.) With a 20-pound propane tank, the generator will run up to 7 hours at 50 percent load.

This is a heavy model, weighing 211 pounds, but it mainly came assembled—all we had to do was attach the wheels and the handle. We tested it first with gasoline, followed by propane, and the results were excellent with both fuels. We ran several power tools simultaneously and powered an oven/range and a clothes dryer (at separate times). A nice perk was the remote fob, which allowed us to start the generator from 90 feet away.

The WGen9500DF is a good pick for those who want an emergency generator to power more than just a couple of cell phones.

Get the Westinghouse home generator at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 3.5/5; Power 4.5/5; Value 5/5

A distinct downside with fuel-powered generators is the inability to run them indoors due to hazardous fumes. Power stations, however, can be used indoors to power several appliances and electronic items, depending on their capacity. The Generac GB2000 is a beefy power backup that provides up to 1,600 running watts of electricity and comes with three standard outlets, four USB ports, and a 12V DC car port. Charging the GB2000 took about 3.5 hours when we plugged it directly into a standard AC outlet.

We also charged it with solar panels, but the day was slightly overcast, which kept it from charging quickly—it took about 5 hours to charge from 28 to 100 percent. A sunnier day or stronger solar panels would likely have charged it more quickly. When fully charged, we used it to run our fridge, a miter saw, lamps, a laptop, and cell phone—not all simultaneously. We made about 20 cuts with the miter saw and noticed no lag in the saw’s power. It took a couple of hours to fully charge the cell phone by placing it on the wireless charging panel at the top of the GB2000.

We left the fridge and laptop plugged in for several hours without depleting the battery—we still had 20 percent when we unplugged them. The Generac is well suited as an emergency backup for essential appliances or a remote power source for tailgating and camping, but at 43 pounds, it’s a bit heavy if you plan to carry it very far on trails.

Get the Generac home generator at The Home Depot or Walmart.

Before testing, we carefully researched more than 40 portable and standby generators and over a dozen high-capacity power stations. We looked at consumer satisfaction, ease of use, price, and versatility. We also considered brand reputation—manufacturers like Champion, Honda, Westinghouse, and Briggs & Stratton are highly respected in the generator industry.

Our goal was to pinpoint models that would suit diverse user needs. This list includes powerful, gas-fueled, and dual-fueled generators in addition to quieter inverters and even solar power stations.

Team members assembled and fueled the generators using the appropriate fuel types. Then we plugged in power tools, home appliances, and electronic devices to see if the generators would produce the advertised wattage. We used an online wattage calculator to help us estimate the correct wattage for testing. In addition, we took note of the noise the generators produced when operating (some models are quieter than others), and we took portability into account.

For each generator, we awarded points based on quality and performance. At the end of testing, we averaged the points to determine which models were best suited to specific applications and users.

Several factors can affect each type of generator’s overall functionality when the power goes out. Keep the following considerations in mind when searching for the best home generator to keep you powered up when severe weather or a natural disaster causes an outage.

Finding the best generator for your power needs involves weighing the four types available. Each type has its own set of pros and cons, and one is likely to suit your home’s specific needs better than the others.

Home standby generators, also called whole-house generators, are large, permanently installed generators that connect to a home’s electrical panel for backup power during an electrical outage. They are equipped with an automatic transfer switch (explained in later sections) that automatically switches on the generator’s power supply when it detects a loss of utility power. Home standby generators are most commonly powered by natural gas or propane, but some diesel models are available.

Home standby generators have the largest power ratings and are usually, though not always, powerful enough to satisfy the electrical demands of an entire home. They can power utilities such as water heaters and central air conditioners. The downside is that they’re the most expensive to purchase and install and require installation by certified professionals. An electrician is needed to connect it to the electrical panel, and a plumber may be required to connect the propane or natural gas line to the generator.

As the name suggests, portable generators are small and can be moved to different locations. Compared to standby options, these are cheap home generators. They can have a wide range of power output ratings. Some may only power a limited number of electrical items and appliances, while large-capacity portable generators may have a 30A outlet for connecting a transfer switch.

Many options are gas-powered generators, but some are powered by diesel or propane. Multifuel generators (dual- and tri-fuel) are powered by multiple fuel sources, including gasoline, diesel, propane, and/or natural gas. Be advised that fuel-powered generators should never be used indoors since the engine can emit a toxic level of CO, leading to sickness or death.

Inverter generators are technically a type of portable generator, but they offer a different set of pros and cons. As opposed to conventional generator engines that constantly operate at the same output rate, inverter generators adapt to power demand.

This makes them more fuel efficient, allowing them to have smaller fuel tanks and more portability than other generators. This efficiency reduces their CO emissions. It also makes them quiet generators, usually only producing around a 60-decibel noise level—the same volume level as a typical conversation.

All of these advantages make them a popular choice among campers and RVers who value silent operation and portability. The disadvantages? Inverter generators are typically more expensive than regular portable generators and generally produce less power.

Portable power stations are essentially battery banks that store electrical power. Instead of using gasoline, diesel, propane, or natural gas, power stations are charged in a standard electrical outlet or via solar panels. Solar-powered power stations are often called solar generators and offer a practically unlimited and renewable power source—just as long as the sun is shining.

These power stations are usually designed to be compact and lightweight for incredible portability. They are also virtually silent when in operation. In addition, they can be safely used indoors since they don’t produce any harmful emissions.

The primary disadvantages are that they’re usually more expensive than conventional portable generators and have significantly lower power output. That being said, they can be used to power a handful of essential appliances during an outage.

A generator’s size equates to the amount of power in watts it can generate, ranging from 800 to greater than 50,000-watt power capacity. Generators are sized in both “peak watts” (also called “starting watts”) and “running watts,” but the running watts rating reveals how many continuous watts the generator can supply to keep the electricity running to the connected items. Peak watts are the number of watts the generator can produce for a few seconds to satisfy the extra demand from starting motor-driven items like power tools.

The running watts rating dictates the number of electrical appliances you can run simultaneously and for how long. Because a generator’s starting watts can be 1,000 to 2,000 watts greater than its running watts, it’s important to understand the difference when determining your home’s power requirements.

To determine the generator size you need, calculate the total number of watts your most essential electrical items consume. All electrical appliances are required to have a label that displays their wattage rating; you simply need to add together the wattage figure listed on each item you want to power during an electrical outage.

Generally speaking, a refrigerator consumes between 700 and 1,200 watts; a window air conditioner consumes around 1,000 watts; a portable space heater consumes about 1,500 watts; and lights can be anywhere between 60 and 600 watts. Most households typically require around 5,000 watts to power the most essential components.

A transfer switch connects a generator to a home’s main electrical panel and allows you to switch, or “transfer,” between grid power and generator power. There are both manual and automatic transfer switches. Manual transfer switches require you to physically switch over the power at your electrical panel when the power goes out, while an automatic transfer switch automatically switches over power from the grid to generator power when it detects a loss of power.

Generators can be equipped with various features that make their operation as convenient as possible. These include:

Along with the various features that contribute to convenience, there are also a few important safety features that many generators incorporate into their design, particularly with regard to CO detection. These include:

Operating a generator isn’t complicated, but there are a few tips you’ll want to keep in mind to ensure effective and safe operation and avoid any harm to yourself or your generator when the power goes out.

First of all, it’s important to use extension cords that are sufficiently powerful. As a general rule, use at least 12-gauge outdoor-rated electrical cords for larger appliances (like refrigerators) and at least 14-gauge cords for everything else. Cord length is also a concern since the voltage drop from cords that are too long can damage or destroy the appliances they’re supplying. Although you’ll want to keep a portable generator outside and away from your home, remember not to exceed a 100-foot extension cord length.

When running a home generator, it’s best to keep it on a level surface. If a generator is placed on a slope or hill, the internal lubrication system could malfunction and lead to premature engine wear and damage. Finally, ensure the generator has cooled down before you refill it since spilling gasoline on a hot engine can cause a fire.

Since generators can be both lifesaving and expensive, it’s natural to have some questions before you’re confident in your decision. To this end, consider the answers to these frequently asked questions. Together with the above shopping considerations, these answers provide you with just about everything you need to know about emergency power generators.

Most municipalities and towns require that you have a permit before a standby generator is installed. However, not all locations have this requirement. Check with your local zoning authority to find out if a permit is required in your community.

To determine the necessary power rating for your generator, add up the wattage of all the appliances you want to run during an electrical outage. As a general rule, a generator should have at least a 5,000-watt capacity to power a home’s essential appliances. But, your home could require substantially more power than that.

Yes, fuel-powered home generators require oil to operate properly without wearing out the moving parts.

Most manufacturers recommend that the whole-house generator be installed at least 5 feet from doors, windows, vents, and any flammable material. There may also be local regulations about the placement of a whole-house generator, so make sure to check local guidelines to ensure that your whole-house generator meets local building codes and installation guidelines.

No. A generator should not be plugged into a house outlet because it is both dangerous and illegal in many locations. This is called backfeeding and it can severely damage the home’s electrical system or even cause a fire. Additionally, any technicians who are working on electrical lines on the same power grid are at increased risk of electrocution.

You can connect a generator to individual appliances using a series of extension cords, or if you want direct power for entire circuits in the home, have a standby generator professionally installed.

On average, it will take an experienced technician about 1 to 2 full days to complete the installation of your whole-house generator. It could take 1 to 2 weeks to prep for the installation, such as pouring a concrete pad and running the wires connecting the generator to the electrical panel.

The exact lifespan depends on the specific product, but in general, the overall lifespan of a whole-house generator is about 1,500 to 3,000 hours.

#8036. “Love to the Point of Invention” – Injured Kitten with a Tiny Toy-Car Wheelchair Finds His Forever Home

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Some kittens steal your heart with their big eyes. Others win you over with their playful antics. And then there's Gelato, a tiny kitten who needed a wheelchair and ended up getting one made from Hot Wheels cars. Yes, really. Human ingenuity and humane creativity to the rescue!

Becoming more mobile in a Hot Wheels wheelchair might seem like a dream come true, but today, Gelato has even more reasons to celebrate: Heâs found his forever home.

Gelato arrived at Cincinnati Animal CARE in Ohio as a stray kitten with a lower-back injury that left him unable to use his hind legs normally. The shelter team wanted to help him move around, but there was a rather inconvenient problem. The wheelchairs they had available were too big for his tiny body.

Now, anyone who has lived with a kitten knows that, besides being irresistibly cute, they can be remarkably determined little creatures. They want to explore everything, investigate every corner, and get involved in whatever their humans are doing. Being unable to move around easily can limit those everyday experiences for the tiny fur balls.

Fortunately, Gelato had people in his corner who weren't about to let his small size stop him from exploring the big world.

The shelter's lead veterinary technician, Mallory Smith, came up with a wonderfully resourceful solution. She built a miniature wheelchair using cardboard, tape, zip ties, wooden rulers, and Hot Wheels toy cars. The first version needed adjustments, but Mallory kept working until the little device was ready to support Gelato as he moved around. While this is certainly quite a unique solution, what isnât unusual is the compassion and creativity behind it. Gelatoâs improvised mobility device is a perfect example of how animal medical care personnel go above and beyond to help patients in need.

Gelato's homemade wheelchair was a clever solution to an immediate problem. However, a makeshift device is not necessarily the best long-term option for a growing kitten with mobility challenges.

Help arrived in the form of an engineer who created a custom 3D-printed wheelchair designed to fit his body and accommodate his growth. The toy cars were gone, but Gelatoâs future mobility was looking more stable.

Gelato got lucky the moment someone refused to give up and asked, "How can we make this work?" This first lucky chance opened him to new opportunities from a wider effort to help one small animal have a better chance at life. Itâs impressive how sometimes sharing an animal's story can make all the difference. A social media post can connect shelters with people who have the skills, resources, or homes that animals need.

Giving Gelato a way to move around was an important first step. And there was another milestone waiting for him: a loving family of his own.

As the story of Gelatoâs unusual mode of transport spread, drawing plenty of social media attention, it also caught the eye of Hope Hollandsworth, a 28-year-old tattoo artist and devoted cat parent. When she first saw a photograph of Gelato during the summer, she felt immediately drawn to him.

Hollandsworth already cared for two cats with spinal injuries, Bread Crumb and Sprinkles. Both have limited use of their hind legs and rely on their front legs for mobility. She understood that caring for cats with special needs could involve extra responsibilities, adjustments, and plenty of patience.

In other words, she wasn't going into this adoption without knowing that life with a disabled cat can look a little different. Cat lovers are abundant, but those experienced in caring for disabled felines? Not quite as plentiful.

Hope wasted no time, adopting Gelato as soon as she met him at the shelter. The five-month-old kitten spent his first night in his new home sleeping in her arms.

Absolutely. A disability does not automatically mean that a cat has a poor quality of life. Cats with mobility challenges can still enjoy affection, play, exploration, food puzzles, comfortable naps, and the company of people they trust.

What really matters is understanding the individual cat's needs and making reasonable adjustments to help them live comfortably.

For a cat with a spinal injury, this may include providing easy access to food, water, resting areas, and litter boxes. Non-slip flooring, ramps, and thoughtfully arranged furniture can also help some cats move around more safely. Depending on the injury, a cat may need help with bladder or bowel function, regular skin checks, or a rehabilitation plan.

These are not small details. Some cats with spinal injuries cannot empty their bladders normally, which can lead to serious complications without very devoted care. A veterinarian can assess bladder function, mobility, sensation, and other concerns, then explain what support the cat will need at home. The real challenge is finding someone with the time and patience to take over these responsibilities on a daily basis.

Hollandsworth's experience with Bread Crumb and Sprinkles gave her a head start.

Gelato will continue receiving therapy in the hope that he may regain some use of his hind legs, but for now, his recovery is uncertain. Spinal injuries vary, and a cat's prognosis depends on several factors, including the extent of the damage and the neurological function that remains.

But Gelato doesn't need a guaranteed recovery to deserve a happy future. He's got somewhere to go, someone to cuddle, and absolutely no need to prove that he can walk to earn his place in the family.

His new family is ready to love and support him, whether or not he ever walks on his own. Hollandsworth put it beautifully: to her, Gelato is already perfect just the way he is.

There is a lot of wisdom in that simple sentiment. We can hope for progress, celebrate small improvements, and pursue appropriate treatment without making an animal's worth depend on how much they recover. Loving others, whether animals, people, or even ourselves, for who they are, exactly as they are, is what we call true love.

#8035. Is Your Dog Weird Enough for Times Square?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Does your pup have a bedtime routine that makes no sense, a suspicious obsession with household objects, or dramatically howl at their own reflection in the oven door? Congratulations. You might be living with a contender for the World's Weirdest Dog. Embark Veterinary has officially launched its search for canine oddballs, inviting pet parents to submit photos and videos of their furballâs most gloriously bizarre behaviors before November 15, 2026. The winning pup will earn the ultimate claim to canine fame: their face on a Times Square billboard, the official title of World's Weirdest Dog, and a $200 gift card.

The contest celebrates the behaviors that make dogs funny, unique, and truly memorable; the ones that make us smile when we think about them, while also highlighting  Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature, which explores how canine DNA may influence behavior.

Sock Thieves, Bathtub Sleepers, and Other Household Oddballs

Furry weirdos have interesting, different habits; Embark's examples include a dog who sleeps upside down in the bathtub, one who carries a sock around without chewing it, and a canine who spins exactly three times before lying down. Not two. Not four. Three.

Then there's the dog who refuses to walk past one particular house, or the dinner diva who won't touch a meal until someone has given it the full restaurant treatment.

Such behaviors are entertaining partly because they are so unique and specific. Most pet parents can share at least one story that would make a perfectly reasonable person wonder what goes on inside that furry little head.

A sock might be a very treasured object, a source of comfort, a reminder of their favorite personâs scent, or simply something fun to carry. A particular walking route might feel uncomfortable for reasons a person cannot detect, most likely a scentâ¦ but then again, who knows? And a bedtime ritual may have started with nothing more mysterious than finding a comfortable position.

Of course, some dogs are just little weirdos, and that's part of their charm. But there's a difference between a pup who has always slept with their legs in the air and one who suddenly starts acting strangely. If your pup begins staring at walls, repeating the same movements, or turning down food when that's not normal for them, don't automatically label it as a new amusing personality trait. Pain, illness, and anxiety can all show up as changes in behavior. If something feels off, put the camera down and call the vet.

Genes can influence behavioral tendencies, but they don't write a complete script for an individual dog's life. Learning and environment play a big role, too, sometimes in ways pet parents never intended.

Take the sock thief. A dog grabs a sock, their pet parents react with dramatic excitement, and suddenly the household is involved in a thrilling chase. From our perspective, it's a laundry crime. From the pup's perspective, it may be an excellent new game.

Behaviors that lead to positive or rewarding outcomes are more likely to happen again. Attention, play, food, and access to preferred activities can all reinforce behavior, even when nobody is training anything on purpose.

Genetics can contribute, too. Inherited tendencies may influence a dog's motivation to chase, retrieve, explore, or seek food. But a predisposition doesn't guarantee a particular behavior, nor does it explain every individual habit. A dog's behavior comes from a combination of biology and learned experience, which is often less convenient than blaming everything on their breed, but it is much closer to reality.

A 2022 study published in Science looked at the behavior and DNA of thousands of dogs. Researchers found that a dog's breed explained only about 9% of the differences in behavior between individual dogs. In other words, dogs of the same breed can have very different personalities and behaviors. Genetics plays a role, but it doesn't tell the whole story.

That doesn't mean genetics is irrelevant. The researchers found evidence that many behavioral traits do have a heritable component. Rather, the findings show why breed alone is a poor crystal ball for predicting how an individual dog will behave.

Some dogs may be especially motivated to retrieve, chase, or investigate, reflecting tendencies shaped partly by their ancestry and breeding history. But individual dogs still vary, and experience helps shape how those tendencies appear. However, with more data, we may learn new things; science is ever evolving along with our technologies.

Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature connects genetic information with behavioral insights and training guidance. Genetic results can be useful, but they are one piece of the puzzle and not a personality prediction.

Behavior is best understood in context. Has the habit been present for years, or did it start last week? What happens before the behavior? Could pain, fear, stress, or another medical issue be contributing?

If a pup is safe and comfortable, there's often no reason to stop a peculiar routine unless itâs a problem. A dog who carries a favorite toy around the house doesn't need a corrective training plan. When a behavior does create a problem, redirection and positive reinforcement can help teach an alternative response without relying on intimidation or punishment. This is the science of behavioral modification.

The goal isn't to turn every pup into a perfectly polished obedience champion, but to help us understand what each dog needs and help them become great family members.

Pet parents can enroll their weirdos through November 15, 2026, by uploading a photo or video of their pup's strangest behavior, with an optional short story, at Embark's official contest page. No weird dog? No problem. You can still get involved by casting your vote for the weirdest dog through the official voting page.

The first-place winner will receive the World's Weirdest Dog title, a Times Square billboard feature, and a $200 gift card. Second through fifth place will receive $150 gift cards each, while sixth through fifteenth place will receive an Embark Breed + Health Dog DNA Test with the Behavior Insights & Training upgrade.

So, if you know your furry pal is a weirdo, this may be their moment. Let that freak flag fly!
